hook: Students who eat breakfast get better grades. Does that mean breakfast raises grades? Maybe, but students who eat breakfast may also sleep more or have more help at home. Before collecting data, you need a clear question and a plan that can answer it. Whether you may claim that breakfast causes anything depends on how the data were collected.

figure.caption: From an investigative question to a plan: a census measures everyone; a sample survey or observational study shows how variables relate; only an experiment supports cause and effect.

chain.cause: Write an investigative question that names the population, the variable and the kind of answer
chain.effect: it tells you what to measure, on whom, and which parameter you are after

chain.cause: If you can measure the whole population
chain.effect: a census answers the question directly

chain.cause: If you observe without imposing anything (a survey or observational study)
chain.effect: you can describe the population and show how variables are related

chain.cause: But groups that form on their own can differ in other ways
chain.effect: confounding blocks a cause-and-effect conclusion; that needs an experiment with conditions decided by chance

ideas: An investigative question names the population, the variable, the parameter (such as a proportion or a typical value) and whether the goal is to describe or to look for a cause.
A census collects data from every member of the population; a sample survey asks questions of a sample.
An observational study records variables without imposing anything (looking back: retrospective; following forward: prospective). An experiment imposes conditions and measures the response.
The explanatory variable may help explain changes in the response variable. A confounding variable is related to both, so its effect cannot be separated.
A cause-and-effect conclusion needs an experiment in which chance decides who gets which condition.

misconception.wrong: Walkers in a study of 1,200 adults had lower blood pressure, so walking lowers blood pressure.
misconception.right: This is an observational study. Walkers may be younger or eat differently, and those confounding variables could explain the difference. Only an experiment supports cause and effect.

summary: An investigative question names the population, the variable, the parameter and the kind of conclusion wanted. A census measures everyone; sample surveys and observational studies record variables without imposing anything, so they show relationships but confounding blocks cause. Only an experiment, with conditions decided by chance, supports a cause-and-effect conclusion.
